Le biais de proportionnalité nous fait c: Proportionality bias makes us believe a big event must have a big cause: that one man alone could have killed Kennedy seems too small. In 2013 Gérald Bronner described the "argumentative mille-feuille": each argument alone is fragile, but people tell themselves it cannot all be false. And believing one conspiracy makes believing others more likely, even contradictory ones: in 2012 the same people found it plausible both that Princess Diana was murdered and that she faked her death.
Des complots réels existent pourtant. De: Real conspiracies do exist, though. From 1932 to 1972 the Tuskegee study denied treatment to Black men with syphilis; Peter Buxtun alerted the press. What separates a real conspiracy from an imagined one: documents, witnesses, evidence.
Grand événement ≠ grande cause. Mille ar: Big event ≠ big cause. A thousand fragile arguments do not make a proof. A real conspiracy is proved (Tuskegee).

Quand un premier chiffre tire nos estima: When a first number pulls our estimates.
Un premier chiffre, même absurde, tire l: A first number, even an absurd one, pulls subsequent estimates toward it.

Les prix barrés et les premières offres: Crossed-out prices and opening offers in a negotiation exploit anchoring.
Même les experts y cèdent : des juges in: Even experts give in to it: judges' sentences influenced by a die roll (Englich, 2006).

Estimation médiane selon le chiffre de l: Median estimate depending on the wheel's number
En 1974, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1974 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a rigged lottery wheel in front of participants, stopping on 10 or 65. Then they asked: what share of UN member countries are African? After 10, the median estimate was 25 %; after 65, 45 %. A number plainly unrelated had pulled the answers towards it.
Autre expérience du même article : en ci: Another experiment from the same article: in five seconds, estimate 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Median: 2,250. In reverse order, 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 8: 512. The first numbers read serve as an anchor. The right answer, 40,320, is far from both.
Un premier chiffre, même absurde, tire l: A first number, even an absurd one, pulls estimates towards it (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974: 25 % against 45 %).
En 1974, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1974 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a rigged lottery wheel in front of participants, stopping on 10 or 65.
Un prix barré à 200 € à côté de 120 € :: A price crossed out at €200 next to €120: the first number serves as a reference, and the second looks like a bargain. The very expensive dish at the top of a restaurant menu is not always there to be sold: it makes the others look reasonable. In negotiation, the first offer anchors the whole discussion. The effect was measured in 1974 by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, with a rigged wheel that stopped on 10 or 65: those who saw 10 estimated the share of African countries in the UN at 25% on average, those who saw 65 at 45%.
Cousin de l'ancrage, l'effet de leurre :: A cousin of anchoring is the decoy effect: a medium popcorn at €6.50 exists mainly to make the large one at €7 look like good value. Nobody wants the medium; it is there for comparison. The effect was described by Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto, in 1982, under the name of asymmetrically dominated alternative. Spotting the option nobody picks is often spotting the decoy.
Prix barré, plat cher en tête de carte,: Crossed-out price, expensive dish at the top of the menu, first offer: anchors. The option nobody takes is often a decoy.
On pourrait croire que l'expérience prot: You might think experience protects. In 2006 Birte Englich and colleagues had experienced judges and prosecutors read a case file, with a requested sentence determined… by dice. The higher the dice roll, the heavier the sentence they proposed.
Et savoir que l'ancre est absurde ne suf: And knowing the anchor is absurd is not enough to break free of it: the effect shrinks a little in people who have been warned, but persists. The best reflex is to make your own estimate before hearing any number, or to look for an independent reference, rather than adjusting from the anchor.
Les experts aussi (juges et dés, Englich: Experts too (judges and dice, Englich, 2006). Estimate before hearing a number, or find an independent reference.
En 2006, Birte Englich et ses collègues: In 2006 Birte Englich and colleagues had experienced judges and prosecutors read a case file, with a requested sentence determined… by dice.
Asch, la pensée de groupe, l'effet Pygma: Asch, groupthink, the Pygmalion effect, the bystander effect: when others think for us.
Asch, 1951 : face à un groupe unanime qu: Asch, 1951: facing a unanimous group in error, 74% give in at least once; a single ally is enough to resist.
Pensée de groupe (Janis, 1972) : un grou: Groupthink (Janis, 1972): a close-knit group stops examining its choices. Bay of Pigs, 1961.

Effet du témoin : la responsabilité se d: Bystander effect: responsibility is diluted in a group; yet in the street, someone almost always helps.
L'effet Pygmalion à l'école existe, mais: The Pygmalion effect at school exists, but it is small and often temporary, far from its legend.
L'influence des autres dans le temps: The influence of others in time
En 1951, au Swarthmore College, Solomon: In 1951, at Swarthmore College, Solomon Asch showed a model line and three lines of different lengths: which one matches the model? Alone, students got it wrong less than once in a hundred. But in the room, all the others were confederates who gave, aloud and unanimously, the same wrong answer.
Sur 12 essais truqués, 74 % des particip: Over 12 rigged trials, 74% of participants gave in at least once, and a little over a third of answers followed the group. But a single ally telling the truth was enough: conformity fell to 5%. Answering in writing also reduced it. Asch worried that intelligent, well-meaning young people were willing to call white black.
Asch, 1951 : face à un groupe unanime qu: Asch, 1951: facing a unanimous group in error, 74% give in at least once. A single ally, or a written answer, is enough to resist.
Seuls, les étudiants se trompent moins d: Alone, students got it wrong less than once in a hundred.
Le mot « groupthink » apparaît en 1952 s: The word "groupthink" appeared in 1952, written by the journalist William H. Whyte in Fortune magazine; he borrowed it from Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four. In 1972, the psychologist Irving Janis, of Yale, turned it into a theory in Victims of Groupthink: a close-knit group, eager to agree, stops examining its choices.
Janis relève huit symptômes, dont l'illu: Janis listed eight symptoms, including the illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship and the illusion of unanimity. Textbook case: in 1961, Kennedy's team accepted without scrutiny the CIA's plan to land in Cuba, at the Bay of Pigs; it was a disaster. In 1962, during the missile crisis, Kennedy brought in outside experts, split the group into subgroups and left the room. Same men, another method.
Whyte, 1952 ; Janis, 1972 : un groupe qu: Whyte, 1952; Janis, 1972: a group that wants to agree stops thinking. Remedies: outside views, subgroups, an absent boss.
Le mot « groupthink » apparaît en 1952 s: The word "groupthink" appeared in 1952, written by the journalist William H. Whyte in Fortune magazine; he borrowed it from Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four.
En 1968, Robert Rosenthal et Lenore Jaco: In 1968, Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson led the teachers of a Californian school to believe that 20% of their pupils, picked at random, were about to bloom. By the end of the study, the youngest of them had progressed more: the "Pygmalion effect". But later studies judged it small and often temporary; it nearly vanishes when the teacher already knows the pupils.
Les autres pèsent aussi sur l'action. En: Others also weigh on action. In 1964, it was said that 38 neighbours let Kitty Genovese be killed without reacting; the figure was false, the New York Times admitted in 2016. But experiments confirm a dilution: alone, 70% of participants help a woman in distress, 40% next to a stranger. In the street, though, cameras show that at least one passer-by intervenes in over 90% of disputes.
Pygmalion (1968) : les attentes pèsent,: Pygmalion (1968): expectations matter, but little and not for long. Bystanders: responsibility is diluted, but in real streets someone almost always helps.
En 1968, Robert Rosenthal et Lenore Jaco: In 1968, Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson led the teachers of a Californian school to believe that 20% of their pupils, picked at random, were about to bloom.

Bartlett, 1932 : la mémoire reconstruit: Bartlett, 1932: memory reconstructs; what does not fit our schemas drops out or changes.
Loftus et Palmer, 1974 : le verbe de la: Loftus and Palmer, 1974: the verb in the question changes the estimated speed and makes people "see" broken glass.
Effet de désinformation : une informatio: Misinformation effect: information received afterwards slips into the memory.
Biais rétrospectif (Fischhoff, 1975) : u: Hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1975): once the outcome is known, we believe we foresaw it.
Être sûr de son souvenir ne prouve rien: Being sure of a memory proves nothing: flashbulb memories are special only in their perceived accuracy.
À Cambridge, Frederic Bartlett fait lire: At Cambridge, Frederic Bartlett had English people read a Native American tale, The War of the Ghosts, then retell it several times, weeks apart. With each version, what seemed strange to them disappeared or became familiar: "canoes" became "boats". The longer the interval, the further the story drifted from the original.
Il en tire, dans Remembering, en 1932, u: In Remembering, in 1932, he drew an idea that would last: memory is not a recording but a reconstruction. We do not replay a memory, we rebuild it from a few traces, guided by schemas, our usual frames, our knowledge and our expectations. Bartlett then held the chair of experimental psychology at Cambridge.
Bartlett, 1932 : se souvenir, c'est reco: Bartlett, 1932: to remember is to reconstruct. What does not fit our schemas drops out or changes (canoes become boats).
À chaque version, ce qui leur semble étr: With each version, what seemed strange to them disappeared or became familiar: "canoes" became "boats".
En 1974, Elizabeth Loftus et John Palmer: In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed 45 students films of car crashes, then asked: how fast were the cars going when they "smashed", "hit", "contacted" each other? With smashed, the mean estimate was about 41 miles per hour; with contacted, about 32. The verb changed what they believed they had seen.
Une semaine plus tard, une autre série d: A week later, another set of participants had to say whether they had seen broken glass. There was none. With "smashed", 32% said yes, against 14% with "hit". In 1978, a false mention of a "Yield" sign replaced in memory the "Stop" sign actually seen: the misinformation effect. Loftus has since testified in more than 300 trials.
Loftus et Palmer, 1974 : « smashed » fai: Loftus and Palmer, 1974: "smashed" raises the speed and makes people see broken glass. Information received afterwards slips into memory.

En 1977, Roger Brown et James Kulik nomm: In 1977, Roger Brown and James Kulik named "flashbulb memories" the memories of the moment one learns shocking news: we think we see it all again, the place, the people, the time. After the Challenger shuttle exploded in 1986, Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch questioned students; three years later, their memories were not very accurate, yet they remained very sure of them.
La mémoire réécrit aussi nos propres pré: Memory also rewrites our own forecasts. In 1975, Baruch Fischhoff described hindsight bias, the "I knew it all along". Before Nixon's trip to Beijing and Moscow, his participants estimated the odds of various events; afterwards, they remembered giving higher odds to what happened. Remedy: explicitly imagine the other possible outcomes.
Souvenirs flash : très vifs, très sûrs,: Flashbulb memories: very vivid, very sure, often wrong. Hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1975): knowing the outcome rewrites what we believed before.

Mesurer ce qu'on sait, et ce qu'on croit: Measuring what you know, and what you think you know.
Effet Dunning-Kruger : les moins compéte: Dunning-Kruger effect: the least competent overestimate their level the most, since they don't know what they don't know.
Les plus compétents ont tendance à se so: The most competent tend to slightly underestimate themselves.
La courbe en « montagne de la stupidité: The “Mount Stupid” curve circulating on the Internet is not in the original paper.
Métacognition : s'entraîner à dire « je: Metacognition: practice saying “I'm 70% sure” and check whether you're right 7 times out of 10.
Dunning-Kruger ne dit pas que les ignora: Dunning-Kruger doesn't say ignorant people think they're experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top.
En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students in logic, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves. Those in the bottom quarter placed themselves on average around the 62nd percentile, when they were near the 12th. The skills they lack are precisely the ones that would let them see their mistakes. The best slightly underestimated themselves.
Attention aux caricatures. Les moins com: Beware of caricatures. The least competent do not think they are experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top, and always below the best. The famous "Mount Stupid" curve does not come from the paper. And some researchers think a good part of the effect is a statistical artefact, linked to regression to the mean; Dunning defends his findings.

En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students in logic, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves.
La métacognition, c'est savoir ce qu'on: Metacognition is knowing what you know, and spotting what you do not. A simple exercise: instead of answering yes or no, say "I'm 70 % sure", then check. If you are right about 7 times out of 10 when you say you are 70 % sure, you are well calibrated. Most people discover they are wrong far more often than they thought at "90 %".
La surconfiance est partout. En 1981, Ol: Overconfidence is everywhere. In 1981 Ola Svenson found that 93 % of the Americans he asked placed themselves in the more skilful half of drivers. And the planning fallacy makes us underestimate how long our projects will take, even when we know previous ones ran late. Conversely, impostor syndrome credits one's successes to luck.
Se calibrer : « sûr à 70 % » doit tomber: Calibrate yourself: "70 % sure" should be right 7 times out of 10. 93 % of drivers think they are in the better half (Svenson, 1981).
En 1981, Ola Svenson trouve que 93 % des: In 1981 Ola Svenson found that 93 % of the Americans he asked placed themselves in the more skilful half of drivers.
Relire un cours donne une impression tro: Rereading a lesson gives a misleading sense of mastery: everything feels familiar, so it seems known. Testing yourself, fetching the answer from memory without looking, strengthens the memory far better. That is the testing effect, or retrieval practice, and it is the very principle of this game.
Il y a aussi un angle mort : nous repéro: There is also a blind spot: we spot other people's biases very well, our own far less. Emily Pronin and colleagues described it in 2002. The more you learn in a field, the more you measure how much you do not know: that is the flip side of Dunning-Kruger, and rather a good sign.
Se tester bat la relecture (effet de tes: Testing beats rereading (testing effect). We see others' biases, not our own (blind spot, Pronin, 2002).
